summary: This informational document explains Self-Delimiting Numeric Values, a field type that encodes arbitrarily large non-negative integers or bit strings compactly. The length is implied by the data, so protocols can grow without fixed field sizes. It was introduced in Delay-Tolerant Networking protocols.

eli5.summary: A number that tells you where it ends, so it can be short when small and long when big, with no wasted space or fixed width.

questions: variable length integer encoding in dtn
how do self-delimiting numeric values work
why use variable length encoding in protocols
subtitle: Variable-length integer encoding that shrinks with the value, avoiding fixed-size field limits.

tldr.problem: Protocol designers must choose a fixed field size for values like sequence numbers, lengths, or identifiers, but oversizing wastes space and undersizing causes scalability problems (like TCP's 64 KB window or IPv4's 32-bit address space).
tldr.mechanism: Self-Delimiting Numeric Values (SDNVs) encode non-negative integers of arbitrary length by using 7 bits of each byte for the value and 1 bit as a continuation flag, allowing the size to grow with the value and the decoder to know when the value ends.
tldr.outcome: Protocols can use SDNVs to avoid painful field-size decisions, providing flexibility and future-proofing without complex negotiation or extension mechanisms, especially useful in delay-tolerant networking where handshaking is expensive.

facts.label: Encoding method
facts.value: 7 bits per byte, with high bit as continuation flag

facts.label: Time complexity
facts.value: O(log n) for both encoding and decoding

facts.label: Primary use
facts.value: DTN protocols (Bundle Protocol, Licklider Transmission Protocol)

today: RFC 6256 is an Informational RFC from the Internet Research Task Force that has not been obsoleted. SDNVs are actively used in DTN protocols and remain the standard variable-length encoding for Delay-Tolerant Networking. While broader adoption in general-purpose Internet protocols has not yet occurred, the RFC provides a foundation for future protocols that may benefit from SDNV's flexibility.

sections.title: The Problem with Fixed Fields
sections.content:
Protocol designers face an optimization problem when choosing field widths. Smaller fields reduce overhead and improve processing speed, but protocols remain in use for decades while technology changes rapidly. History shows painful consequences: TCP's 16-bit advertised receive window limited throughput on high-speed networks until the Window Scale option was added; IPv4's 32-bit address space eventually ran out, driving the need for Network Address Translation and IPv6.

These fixed-size decisions seemed reasonable at design time but became restrictive as networks grew. Protocol designers need flexibility to handle values of unknown or variable magnitude without negotiating field sizes (which is expensive in delay-tolerant networks) or creating extension mechanisms (which add complexity). SDNVs provide a simple alternative: encode values compactly when small, expanding only as needed.
sections.eli5: When you first design a protocol, you have to guess: 'How big will this number ever get?' Pick too small and the number does not fit. Pick too big and you waste space forever. SDNV says: 'Use only as many bytes as the number needs.'

sections.title: How SDNVs Work
sections.content:
An SDNV encodes a non-negative integer by representing it as a string of bits, padding to a multiple of 7 bits if needed. The bits are then divided into 7-bit chunks and packed into bytes. The high-order bit of each byte is a continuation flag: a '0' means it is the last byte, a '1' means more bytes follow. The remaining 7 bits of each byte hold the next 7 bits of the value, left-to-right.

For example, the decimal number 1 is the 7-bit string '0000001' and encodes as a single byte 0x01 (with the high bit clear). The number 128 is the 14-bit string '10000001 00000000' and encodes as two bytes: 0x81 (high bit set to indicate continuation, 7 bits '0000001') followed by 0x00 (high bit clear to end, 7 bits '0000000'). The decoding process reverses this: read bytes, extract the 7 low bits, shift left by 7 and accumulate, and stop when the high bit is clear.
sections.eli5: Split a number into 7-bit pieces. Put each piece in a byte. Mark all bytes except the last one with a continuation bit that says 'more bytes coming'. When reading, keep grabbing bytes and piecing them together until you hit one without the continuation bit set.

sections.title: Why SDNVs for Delay-Tolerant Networking
sections.content:
Delay-Tolerant Networking (DTN) uses SDNVs in protocols like the Bundle Protocol and Licklider Transmission Protocol (LTP) for fields such as identifiers, payload lengths, and sequence numbers. DTN is designed for networks with very high latency (like interplanetary communication) where links have low capacity and nodes cannot be easily upgraded. SDNVs are ideal in this context because they avoid unnecessary header overhead.

In a 64-bit fixed field, a small value like 100 wastes 63 bits. In an SDNV, that same value takes only one byte. For interplanetary spacecraft, where every bit counts and upgrading on-board software is nearly impossible, this matters. Furthermore, DTN protocols must avoid handshaking to establish field widths, since acknowledgment delays are enormous. SDNVs are self-explaining: the format itself reveals the length, requiring no prior negotiation.
sections.eli5: Space probes cannot phone home and ask 'How big should I make this field?' They must send their data in a format that works forever without asking permission. SDNV works forever because the data tells you when it ends.

sections.title: Encoding and Decoding Algorithms
sections.content:
The encoding algorithm is straightforward. Set a variable X to the least significant 7 bits of the number, with the high bit clear. Set Y to the number right-shifted by 7 bits. If Y is zero, X is the result. Otherwise, set Z to the bitwise OR of 0x80 (the continuation bit) with the 7 least significant bits of Y, append Z to X, right-shift Y by 7 bits, and repeat. This process runs in O(log n) time and requires no extra space beyond the result.

Decoding is trickier because the result length is unknown in advance. Initialize the result to 0. Read the first byte, shift the result left by 7 bits, and add the low 7 bits of the byte to the result. If the high bit of the byte is set, advance to the next byte and repeat. If the high bit is clear, return the result. Protocols must specify a maximum SDNV size to ensure decoders do not overflow. The algorithm handles variable-size results by potentially reallocating memory as more data arrives, but implementations often avoid this by pre-allocating based on the protocol's declared maximum.
sections.eli5: Encoding: take 7 bits at a time from the number, put each in a byte, mark all but the last with a 'more' flag. Decoding: read a byte, grab its 7 bits, shift left and add them to the result, and if there is a 'more' flag, read the next byte.

sections.title: Comparison and Trade-offs
sections.content:
SDNVs resemble variable-length encoding schemes in ASN.1 (the Basic Encoding Rules), which have been used for decades in telecommunications for the same reason. For very large values (like 1024-bit RSA keys), SDNVs are inefficient: they add 1/8 of the bits as overhead, while a fixed-size field would have none. For this reason, a best practice is to use SDNV only for the length field in a Type-Length-Value structure, avoiding large numbers in direct SDNV encoding.

Protocol designers must be aware that SDNV encoding may discard leading zero bits, and decoders may add them when padding to machine-word boundaries. When SDNVs encode bitfields (rather than pure integers), senders and receivers must have consistent width interpretation, either through protocol version agreements, explicit width fields, or bit-marking conventions. Most protocols successfully use SDNVs for identifiers, lengths, sequence numbers, and nonces. No IETF transport or network-layer protocol outside of DTN has adopted SDNVs as of the RFC publication, though the authors see no fundamental reason they could not be used more broadly.
sections.eli5: SDNV works best for most values, but for huge numbers it adds a little overhead. Also, both sides must agree on how many bits represent the value, or they might disagree on what it means.

data.title: Example SDNV values
data.code:
Value 1:        Bits 0000001        → Byte 0x01
Value 127:      Bits 01111111      → Byte 0x7F
Value 128:      Bits 10000001 0     → Bytes 0x81 0x00
Value 300:      Bits 100101100     → Bytes 0x82 0x2C
Value 16384:    Bits 1 00000000000000 → Bytes 0x80 0x80 0x00
